subject: biology
title: D2.3 Water potential
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: D2.3 Water potential — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic D2.3.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering D2.3 Water potential, guide topic D2.3.
final_note: You worked through D2.3 Water potential — 11 guide statements.

concepts.def: The process in which solute particles become separated from one another and surrounded by solvent molecules, so that the solute dissolves. With water as the solvent, solvation depends on the polarity of water: the oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogen atoms partial positive charges, so water molecules are attracted to charged ions and to polar molecules.

concepts.term: Hydrogen bonding between water and polar solutes
concepts.def: The attraction that holds polar molecules such as glucose in solution: hydrogen bonds form between the partially charged atoms of water molecules and polar groups on the solute, for example the hydroxyl (–OH) groups of a sugar. Non-polar molecules such as triglycerides have no such groups, so water cannot form hydrogen bonds with them and they do not dissolve.

The attraction of polar water molecules to charged ions when an ionic compound dissolves. Positively charged ions such as Na⁺ are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and negatively charged ions such as Cl⁻ are attracted to the partially positive hydrogen atoms. Each ion becomes surrounded by a shell of oriented water molecules that keeps it separated from other ions.

The net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration. The direction is expressed in terms of solute concentration: water moves from the hypotonic solution to the hypertonic solution.

A solution that has a lower solute concentration than the solution it is being compared with, such as the cytoplasm of a cell. Water moves by osmosis out of a hypotonic solution into the solution with which it is compared.

A solution that has a higher solute concentration than the solution it is being compared with, such as the cytoplasm of a cell. Water moves by osmosis into a hypertonic solution from the solution with which it is compared.

A solution that has the same solute concentration as the solution it is being compared with. There is no net movement of water by osmosis between two isotonic solutions, although water molecules continue to cross the membrane in both directions.

The state of a cell in an isotonic environment: water molecules cross the membrane into and out of the cell at equal rates, so there is no net movement of water even though individual molecules are moving in both directions all the time. This is different from water movement stopping.

concepts.term: Isotonic solute concentration of a tissue
concepts.def: The solute concentration of a bathing solution at which plant tissue shows no net change in mass or length, because the solution is isotonic with the cells. It is deduced from the results of bathing samples of tissue in a range of concentrations: percentage change in mass or length is plotted against concentration, and the isotonic concentration is where the line crosses zero change, which is usually between two of the concentrations tested rather than one of them.

A statistic that describes the spread of a set of repeat measurements around their mean. A small standard deviation shows that the repeats are close together; a large one shows they are widely scattered. In the plant-tissue experiment it can be calculated for the repeats at each concentration and used to compare the reliability of length measurements with the reliability of mass measurements.

A statistic that indicates how close the mean of a sample of repeats is likely to be to the true mean. It is smaller than the standard deviation of the same data and becomes smaller as the number of repeats increases. Standard error can be shown on a graph as error bars extending above and below each plotted mean.

The shrinkage of a cell that lacks a cell wall when it is placed in a hypertonic medium: water leaves the cell by osmosis, its volume decreases and the cell membrane develops a crinkled, scalloped outline. In a hypotonic medium the same kind of cell swells and can burst, because there is no wall to resist its expansion.

A membrane-bound structure in freshwater unicellular organisms such as Paramecium that fills with water and then contracts to expel it from the cell. Because the cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, water enters the cell continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole removes it, preventing the cell from swelling and bursting.

The condition that multicellular organisms maintain in the fluid surrounding their cells so that the cells, which lack walls, neither gain water and burst nor lose water and shrink. Keeping tissue fluid isotonic with the cytoplasm prevents these harmful changes.

The pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall of a plant cell that has taken in water by osmosis in a hypotonic medium. The wall resists expansion, so pressure builds up inside the cell until net uptake of water stops; the cell is then turgid. Turgor pressure is what makes non-woody plant tissue firm.

The condition of a plant cell in a hypertonic medium: water leaves the cell by osmosis, the protoplast (the cell contents inside the membrane) shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. The wall itself keeps its shape, and the space between wall and membrane is filled by the external solution, which passes freely through the wall.

Fluid given into a patient's vein during medical treatment, for example 0.9% sodium chloride solution (normal saline), which is isotonic with blood plasma. Because it has the same solute concentration as the plasma, the patient's blood cells neither take in water and burst nor lose water and crenate; pure water could not be given for this reason.

concepts.term: Isotonic bathing of organs for transplantation
concepts.def: The practice of storing an organ that has been removed for transplantation in a solution isotonic with the cytoplasm of its cells. This prevents net osmotic movement of water into or out of the cells, so they are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before the organ is transplanted.

The potential energy of water per unit volume. It indicates the tendency of water to move: water moves from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. The units are usually kilopascals (kPa).

Pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, which is assigned a water potential of zero. The absolute quantity of potential energy in water cannot be measured, so water potentials are always given relative to this reference. Dissolving solutes lowers water potential, so every solution at atmospheric pressure has a negative water potential.

A difference in water potential between two regions. Water moves down the gradient, from the region of higher water potential to the region of lower water potential, because in doing so it loses potential energy; the movement needs no input of energy from a cell. Net movement stops when the two regions have the same water potential.

The contribution of dissolved solutes to water potential. Solute potential is zero for pure water and becomes more negative as solute concentration increases, so it ranges from zero downwards and is negative for every solution.

The contribution of pressure to water potential. Inside plant cells pressure potential is generally positive, because the cell wall presses back on the contents of a cell that has taken in water. In xylem vessels where sap is being transported under tension, pressure potential is negative.

ψw = ψs + ψp: the water potential of a cell with a wall is the sum of its solute potential and its pressure potential. Because ψs is zero or negative and ψp inside a cell is usually positive, a cell's water potential is less negative than its solute potential; for example, ψs = −700 kPa and ψp = +200 kPa give ψw = −500 kPa.

The state of a plant cell bathed in a hypotonic solution such as pure water once net uptake of water has stopped. Water entering the cell raises the pressure potential as the wall resists expansion; at full turgor in pure water the pressure potential has risen until it equals the magnitude of the solute potential, so ψw = ψs + ψp = 0, the same as the water outside, and there is no further net movement.

The point reached by a plant cell losing water to a hypertonic solution at which the protoplast has just stopped pressing on the cell wall. The pressure potential has fallen to zero, so the cell's water potential equals its solute potential (ψw = ψs). If the external solution has a still lower water potential, water continues to leave and the membrane pulls away from the wall.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride dissolves when it is placed in water. Which statement describes the attractions that hold the ions in solution?
options: Na⁺ ions are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and Cl⁻ ions to the partially positive hydrogen atoms.
Hydrogen bonds form between each ion and the water molecules that surround it, just as they form between water molecules.
Both kinds of ion are attracted to the oxygen end of the water molecules, because that is the end that carries a charge.
Water molecules react chemically with the sodium chloride, breaking it down into separate sodium and chlorine atoms.
mcqs.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
mcqs.explain: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.
rationales: Water is polar. Each positively charged Na⁺ ion is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of surrounding water molecules, and each negatively charged Cl⁻ ion to the partially positive hydrogen atoms, so the ions are separated and held in solution.

A student who uses hydrogen bonding to explain every property of water picks this. Hydrogen bonds form between water and polar molecules such as glucose; an ion is held in solution by the attraction between its charge and the partial charges on water.

A student who has only seen a hydrated sodium ion drawn picks this. The hydrogen atoms of water carry partial positive charges, so it is the hydrogen end that is attracted to a negatively charged chloride ion.
A student who thinks of dissolving as a chemical change picks this. No reaction occurs: the ions stay as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and are simply separated and surrounded by water molecules.

mcqs.q: A student writes: "Glucose and sodium chloride both dissolve in water because water molecules form hydrogen bonds with them." How should this claim be evaluated?
options: Correct for both: hydrogen bonds are the attraction that holds every kind of dissolved particle in solution, whether it is a molecule or an ion.
Correct for glucose, whose hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, but not for sodium chloride, whose ions are attracted to water's partial charges.
Incorrect for both: glucose dissociates into ions when it dissolves, and ions are held in solution by attraction to the partial charges on water, not by hydrogen bonds.
Incorrect for both: water dissolves each of these solutes by reacting with it and breaking its molecules or ions apart into smaller particles.
mcqs.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
mcqs.explain: Glucose is a polar molecule with –OH groups that hydrogen-bond to water, so the claim is right for it. Sodium chloride dissolves because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the oppositely charged ends of polar water molecules, which is a different kind of attraction.
rationales: A student who treats hydrogen bonding as the explanation for all solvation picks this. Ions do not form hydrogen bonds; they are held by the attraction between their full charge and the partial charges of polar water molecules.

Glucose is a polar molecule with –OH groups that hydrogen-bond to water, so the claim is right for it. Sodium chloride dissolves because Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the oppositely charged ends of polar water molecules, which is a different kind of attraction.

A student who believes only charged particles can dissolve picks this. Glucose molecules stay intact in solution; their polar hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so the claim is right for glucose.

A student who regards dissolving as a chemical reaction picks this. Solvation is physical: glucose molecules and sodium and chloride ions are surrounded by water molecules but are not broken down or changed.

mcqs.q: Two sucrose solutions, 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and 0.6 mol dm⁻³, are separated by a membrane that is permeable to water but not to sucrose. Which statement is correct?
options: Water moves by osmosis from the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution into the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution, down the concentration gradient.
Water moves by osmosis from the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution, which is hypertonic, into the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution, which is hypotonic.
Water moves by osmosis from the hypotonic 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution into the hypertonic 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution.
Sucrose moves from the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution into the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution until the two solutions are isotonic.
mcqs.specStatementText: Osmosis: water moves towards the higher solute concentration
mcqs.explain: Water moves from the less concentrated to the more concentrated solution. The 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution has the lower solute concentration, so it is hypotonic; the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution is hypertonic and gains water.
rationales: A student who applies the diffusion rule 'high to low' to the solution rather than the solute picks this. Water moves from the solution with the lower solute concentration to the solution with the higher solute concentration.
A student who has swapped the prefixes picks this. The direction is right, but the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution has the lower solute concentration and is hypotonic; the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution is hypertonic.

Water moves from the less concentrated to the more concentrated solution. The 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution has the lower solute concentration, so it is hypotonic; the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution is hypertonic and gains water.
A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The membrane is not permeable to sucrose, which is exactly why it is water that moves.

mcqs.q: The cytoplasm of a red blood cell has a solute concentration equivalent to 0.9% sodium chloride. A red blood cell is placed in a 3% sodium chloride solution. What is the net movement across its membrane, and what happens to the cell?
options: Water moves into the cell and it swells, because water moves from the more concentrated solution to the less concentrated cytoplasm.
Water moves into the cell and it swells, because the 3% solution is hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cell.
Sodium chloride moves into the cell until the solute concentrations on the two sides are equal, and the cell's volume is unchanged.
Water moves out of the cell, because the solution is hypertonic to the cytoplasm, so the cell shrinks and becomes crenated.
mcqs.specStatementText: Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
mcqs.explain: The 3% solution has a higher solute concentration than the 0.9%-equivalent cytoplasm, so it is hypertonic to the cell. Net movement of water by osmosis is out of the cell into the hypertonic solution; the cell, which has no wall, shrinks and its membrane develops the crinkled outline called crenation.
rationales: A student who moves water down the solution's concentration gradient picks this. Water moves from the lower solute concentration (the cytoplasm) to the higher solute concentration (the 3% solution), so it leaves the cell and the cell shrinks.
A student who has swapped hypo- and hyper- picks this. The 3% solution has the higher solute concentration, so it is hypertonic to the cytoplasm; water moves out of the cell and it shrinks.

A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The cell membrane is partially permeable: the net movement that reduces the difference is water leaving the cell, which therefore shrinks.

The 3% solution has a higher solute concentration than the 0.9%-equivalent cytoplasm, so it is hypertonic to the cell. Net movement of water by osmosis is out of the cell into the hypertonic solution; the cell, which has no wall, shrinks and its membrane develops the crinkled outline called crenation.

mcqs.q: A cell is placed in a solution that is isotonic with its cytoplasm. Which statement describes the movement of water across its membrane?
options: Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions at equal rates, so there is a dynamic equilibrium with no net movement.
Water molecules stop crossing the membrane in either direction, because there is no concentration gradient to drive them.
Solute molecules cross the membrane in both directions, keeping the concentrations on the two sides of the membrane equal.
The cell stops pumping water across the membrane, because it no longer needs to use energy to adjust its water content.
mcqs.specStatementText: Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
mcqs.explain: In an isotonic environment water molecules continue to enter and leave the cell, but at the same rate. This is a dynamic equilibrium: there is no net movement of water, not an absence of movement.
rationales: In an isotonic environment water molecules continue to enter and leave the cell, but at the same rate. This is a dynamic equilibrium: there is no net movement of water, not an absence of movement.
A student who drops the word 'net' picks this. Individual water molecules move randomly through the membrane whatever the concentrations; the gradient only decides whether there is a net direction.

A student who thinks of concentration differences as being managed by the solute picks this. The membrane is partially permeable, and the question concerns water, which crosses in both directions at equal rates.
A student who believes the cell actively controls osmosis picks this. Osmosis is passive and uses no energy; water crosses the membrane continuously in both directions in an isotonic solution.

mcqs.q: Potato cylinders were bathed for 24 hours in sucrose solutions and their mean percentage change in mass recorded: 0.0 mol dm⁻³, +8.0%; 0.2 mol dm⁻³, +2.5%; 0.4 mol dm⁻³, −3.0%; 0.6 mol dm⁻³, −8.5%; 0.8 mol dm⁻³, −12.0%. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: The isotonic concentration is exactly 0.2 mol dm⁻³, because that is the tested concentration with the change in mass closest to zero.
The potato cells are isotonic with sucrose of about 0.3 mol dm⁻³, the concentration at which the change in mass would be zero.
The 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution was hypotonic to the potato cells, which is why the cylinders bathed in it lost mass.
The cylinders changed in mass because sucrose diffused across their membranes until its concentration was equal on each side.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
mcqs.explain: Mass rose in 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and fell in 0.4 mol dm⁻³, so the line joining the points crosses zero between them. Interpolating between +2.5% and −3.0% gives about 0.29 mol dm⁻³: the concentration isotonic with the cell contents.
rationales: A student who thinks the answer must be one of the tested values picks this. Mass still increased by 2.5% at 0.2 mol dm⁻³, so that solution was hypotonic to the tissue; the isotonic concentration lies between 0.2 and 0.4 mol dm⁻³.

Mass rose in 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and fell in 0.4 mol dm⁻³, so the line joining the points crosses zero between them. Interpolating between +2.5% and −3.0% gives about 0.29 mol dm⁻³: the concentration isotonic with the cell contents.

A student who has swapped the prefixes picks this. The cylinders lost mass because water left their cells, which means the solution had the higher solute concentration: it was hypertonic to the cells.

A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The cell membranes are partially permeable and sucrose cannot cross them; the changes in mass are water entering the cells by osmosis in the hypotonic solutions and leaving them in the hypertonic ones.

mcqs.q: Five potato cylinders were bathed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. Their percentage changes in mass had a mean of −3.0%, a standard deviation of 1.0% and a standard error of 0.45%. What does the standard error indicate?
options: The average size of the mistakes made in weighing the cylinders, which would be zero if the balance had been used correctly.
The spread of the five individual percentage changes around their mean, which is the same thing that the standard deviation shows.
How close the sample mean of −3.0% is likely to be to the true mean; it would decrease if more cylinders were measured.
The maximum and minimum percentage changes recorded, so every cylinder lost between 2.55% and 3.45% of its mass.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
mcqs.explain: Standard error indicates the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the true mean for this concentration. It is smaller than the standard deviation and falls as the number of repeats rises, and it can be shown graphically as error bars.
rationales: A student who reads 'error' as 'mistake' picks this. Standard error reflects natural variation between samples, not faults in technique; perfectly weighed cylinders that vary in their response still give a standard error above zero.

A student who treats the two statistics as one picks this. The spread of the individual values is described by the standard deviation of 1.0%; the standard error is a property of the mean, which is why it is smaller.

Standard error indicates the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the true mean for this concentration. It is smaller than the standard deviation and falls as the number of repeats rises, and it can be shown graphically as error bars.
A student who reads error bars as a range picks this. Standard error is not the limits of the data: with a standard deviation of 1.0%, individual cylinders lie well outside 0.45% of the mean.

mcqs.q: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. What happens to them, and why?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell until their membranes are stretched taut, and then they remain turgid.
Water leaves by osmosis, because the cytoplasm is more concentrated than the distilled water, and the cells shrink.
Water leaves by osmosis, because distilled water is hypertonic to the cytoplasm, and the cells crenate.
Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell and burst, because no wall resists their expansion.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
mcqs.explain: Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water enters the cells by osmosis. Red blood cells lack a cell wall, so nothing resists the increase in volume and the cells swell and burst.
rationales: A student who expects animal cells to behave like plant cells picks this. A cell membrane cannot resist the pressure that a cell wall resists, so the swelling continues until the cell bursts.
A student who moves water from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side picks this. Water moves towards the higher solute concentration, so it enters the cells.

A student who has swapped the prefixes picks this. Distilled water contains no solute, so it is hypotonic to the cytoplasm; crenation happens in a hypertonic medium such as concentrated salt solution.
Distilled water is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water enters the cells by osmosis. Red blood cells lack a cell wall, so nothing resists the increase in volume and the cells swell and burst.

mcqs.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Its contractile vacuole repeatedly fills with water and then expels it from the cell. Why is this necessary?
options: The cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, so water continually enters by osmosis and must be expelled to prevent swelling and bursting.
The vacuole stores the water the cell absorbs, keeping a reserve that the cell can draw on when the pond water becomes scarce.
The vacuole takes in water to replace the water the cell loses by osmosis to the fresh water, which is more dilute than the cytoplasm.
The vacuole is the pump by which the cell moves water in by osmosis, using energy whenever the cytoplasm needs more water.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
mcqs.explain: Fresh water has a much lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water enters the cell by osmosis all the time. Paramecium has no cell wall, and the contractile vacuole removes the water so that the cell does not swell and burst.
rationales: Fresh water has a much lower solute concentration than the cytoplasm, so water enters the cell by osmosis all the time. Paramecium has no cell wall, and the contractile vacuole removes the water so that the cell does not swell and burst.
A student who associates vacuoles with storage picks this. The contractile vacuole expels water from the cell; its job is removal of excess water, not storage.

A student who moves water from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side picks this. Water moves into the more concentrated cytoplasm, so the cell gains water and the vacuole has to remove it.
A student who thinks the cell controls osmosis actively picks this. Osmosis is passive and brings water in unasked; the energy used by the contractile vacuole goes into pushing that water out.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the tissue fluid that bathes the cells of a mammal is correct?
options: It is kept slightly hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they are kept fully hydrated by a steady inflow of water.
It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they neither swell and burst nor shrink through net osmosis.
It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that no water molecules cross their membranes at all.
Its concentration does not need regulating, because cells that take in excess water become turgid and then stop.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
mcqs.explain: Cells without walls are damaged by net water movement in either direction. Multicellular organisms maintain isotonic tissue fluid so that there is a dynamic equilibrium and no harmful change in cell volume.
rationales: A student who thinks more water is always better for cells picks this. A steady inflow of water into cells that lack walls would make them swell and eventually burst.

Cells without walls are damaged by net water movement in either direction. Multicellular organisms maintain isotonic tissue fluid so that there is a dynamic equilibrium and no harmful change in cell volume.
A student who thinks isotonic means no movement picks this. Water molecules cross the membranes continuously; in an isotonic fluid they do so at equal rates in each direction, giving no net movement.
A student who expects animal cells to become turgid picks this. Turgidity depends on a cell wall; animal cells have none, so excess water makes them swell and burst.

mcqs.q: A strip of onion epidermis is mounted in a concentrated sucrose solution and viewed under a microscope. Which statement describes what happens to its cells?
options: Water leaves each cell by osmosis and the whole cell, wall included, shrinks and crumples inward, just as an animal cell crenates.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis and an empty space forms between the wall and the membrane, because the wall lets nothing through.
Water leaves each cell by osmosis, the protoplast shrinks and its membrane pulls away from the wall: the cells are plasmolysed.
Water enters each cell by osmosis, because the concentrated solution is hypotonic to them, and the cells become turgid.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
mcqs.explain: The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.
rationales: A student who transfers crenation to plant cells picks this. The rigid cellulose wall keeps its shape; only the protoplast inside it shrinks.
A student who treats the wall as a barrier picks this. The cell wall is freely permeable, so the space that opens up is filled by the sucrose solution.

The concentrated sucrose solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water leaves by osmosis. The protoplast shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall, which keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis.
A student who has swapped hypo- and hyper- picks this. A concentrated solution has the higher solute concentration, so it is hypertonic and water leaves the cells.

mcqs.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
options: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells until it bursts, like an animal cell in pure water.
Solutes leave the cell into the pure water until the cell sap is as dilute as the water outside.
The cell pumps water in, using energy, until it is full and then it switches the pumping off.
Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid, its wall resisting further expansion.
mcqs.specStatementText: Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
mcqs.explain: Pure water is hypotonic to the cell sap, so water enters by osmosis. The cell wall resists expansion, turgor pressure develops, and net uptake of water stops when the cell is turgid.
rationales: A student who transfers the fate of a red blood cell to a plant cell picks this. The cellulose wall resists expansion, so pressure builds up inside and net entry of water stops before the cell can burst.
A student who expects the solute to equalise the concentrations picks this. The membrane is partially permeable; it is water that moves, entering the cell.

A student who believes the cell drives osmosis actively picks this. Osmosis is passive: water enters down the gradient, and it is the pressure from the wall, not a decision by the cell, that stops net uptake.
Pure water is hypotonic to the cell sap, so water enters by osmosis. The cell wall resists expansion, turgor pressure develops, and net uptake of water stops when the cell is turgid.

mcqs.q: A patient who has lost a large volume of blood is given fluid intravenously. Why is 0.9% sodium chloride solution chosen rather than pure water?
options: It is isotonic with blood plasma, so the patient's blood cells neither take in water and burst nor lose water and crenate.
Pure water would be absorbed too slowly by the blood cells, whereas the sodium chloride solution enters them quickly.
The patient has lost salt along with the blood, and the purpose of the solution is to replace that salt in the plasma.
Pure water is hypertonic to blood plasma, so it would draw water out of the patient's blood cells, shrinking them.
mcqs.specStatementText: Isotonic solutions in medicine
mcqs.explain: 0.9% sodium chloride has the same solute concentration as blood plasma. Adding it to the blood does not change the plasma's solute concentration, so there is no net osmotic movement of water into or out of the blood cells.
rationales: 0.9% sodium chloride has the same solute concentration as blood plasma. Adding it to the blood does not change the plasma's solute concentration, so there is no net osmotic movement of water into or out of the blood cells.

A student who sees pure water as harmless picks this. The problem with pure water is the opposite: it is hypotonic to the cytoplasm, so water would enter the blood cells rapidly by osmosis and burst them.
A student who looks for a nutritional reason picks this. The concentration is chosen for an osmotic reason: it matches the plasma, so fluid can be added without changing its solute concentration.
A student who has swapped the prefixes picks this. Pure water contains no solute, so it is hypotonic to plasma; the danger is that water enters the cells and they burst.

mcqs.q: A kidney removed for transplantation is bathed in a solution while it is stored. Which type of solution is used, and why?
options: Sterile distilled water, so that the cells stay well hydrated and no solutes can enter the organ before it is transplanted.
An isotonic solution, so that the kidney's cells neither gain nor lose water by net osmosis while the organ is stored.
A slightly hypotonic solution, so that the cells are kept fully hydrated by a steady inward flow of water.
A hypotonic solution, so that the cells take in water and become turgid, keeping the organ firm during storage.
mcqs.specStatementText: Isotonic solutions in medicine
mcqs.explain: A solution with the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm of the kidney's cells prevents net osmotic movement of water in either direction, so the cells are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before transplantation.
rationales: A student who regards pure water as the safest fluid picks this. Distilled water is hypotonic to the cells, which would take in water by osmosis, swell and burst.

A solution with the same solute concentration as the cytoplasm of the kidney's cells prevents net osmotic movement of water in either direction, so the cells are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before transplantation.
A student who thinks extra water is good for cells picks this. A hypotonic solution would cause a net inflow of water into cells that lack walls, and they would swell and burst.
A student who expects animal cells to become turgid picks this. Turgidity needs a cell wall; the cells of a kidney have none, so water entering them causes swelling and bursting, not firmness.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes water potential and the scale on which it is measured?
options: It is the absolute potential energy of water per unit volume, so pure water at 20°C has a value of zero because its molecules have no potential energy.
It is the potential energy of water per unit volume, which is zero for pure water and rises to positive values as more and more solute is dissolved in it.
It is the potential energy of water per unit volume, measured in kPa relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, which is set at zero.
It is the concentration of water in a solution, measured in mol dm⁻³, which is highest in pure water and is lower in every other solution.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water potential: energy per unit volume, measured against pure water
mcqs.explain: Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume. Because its absolute quantity cannot be measured, values are expressed relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, defined as zero, and the units are usually kilopascals.
rationales: A student who reads zero as 'none' picks this. The absolute potential energy of water cannot be measured; zero is a chosen reference point, and values are given relative to it.
A student who expects 'more solute' to give a bigger number picks this. Dissolving solute lowers water potential, so solutions at atmospheric pressure have negative values.

Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume. Because its absolute quantity cannot be measured, values are expressed relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, defined as zero, and the units are usually kilopascals.

A student who carries the 'water concentration' model into Higher Level picks this. Water potential is an energy per unit volume, measured in kPa; it also takes account of pressure, which a concentration cannot.

mcqs.q: Two adjacent plant cells have water potentials of −300 kPa (cell A) and −900 kPa (cell B). Which statement describes the net movement of water between them?
options: From B to A, because −900 kPa is the larger number, so the water in B has the greater potential energy.
There is no net movement, because both values are negative, so neither cell's water has any potential energy.
From A to B only if the cells use energy to pump it, because water cannot move down a gradient by itself.
From A to B, because water moves from higher to lower water potential and loses potential energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water moves from higher to lower water potential
mcqs.explain: −300 kPa is the higher water potential, so cell A's water has more potential energy per unit volume than cell B's. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, losing potential energy as it does so, until the two are equal.
rationales: A student who compares magnitudes and ignores the sign picks this. −900 kPa is further below zero than −300 kPa, so B has the lower water potential and its water has less potential energy.
A student who treats the scale as absolute picks this. Negative values are relative to pure water; the water in both cells has potential energy, and there is more of it in A than in B.
A student who thinks water movement is active picks this. Water moves down a water potential gradient passively, without any input of energy from the cells.

−300 kPa is the higher water potential, so cell A's water has more potential energy per unit volume than cell B's. Water moves from higher to lower water potential, losing potential energy as it does so, until the two are equal.

mcqs.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −700 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. What is its water potential?
options: -500 kPa
-900 kPa
-700 kPa
+500 kPa
mcqs.specStatementText: Solute and pressure potentials add up: ψw = ψs + ψp
mcqs.explain: ψw = ψs + ψp = (−700 kPa) + (+200 kPa) = −500 kPa. The positive pressure potential raises the water potential of the cell above its solute potential.
rationales: ψw = ψs + ψp = (−700 kPa) + (+200 kPa) = −500 kPa. The positive pressure potential raises the water potential of the cell above its solute potential.
A student who adds the two values as magnitudes picks this. The pressure potential is positive and the solute potential negative, so they partly cancel: −700 + 200 = −500 kPa.
A student who ignores pressure and equates water potential with solute potential picks this. The wall's pressure on the contents contributes +200 kPa, giving −500 kPa.
A student who expects the water potential of cell contents to be positive picks this. Solute potential is negative, and here it outweighs the pressure potential, so the water potential is −500 kPa.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the solute potential and pressure potential of water in plant structures is correct?
options: Pressure potential is positive throughout the plant, including in the xylem vessels, because a pressure lower than zero cannot exist in a liquid.
Solute potential is zero for pure water and negative for any solution; pressure potential is usually positive in cells but negative in xylem sap under tension.
Solute potential is positive in cell sap, because dissolving solutes adds potential energy to the water, and it is negative only in xylem sap.
Pressure potential makes no contribution to the water potential of a cell; only the solute potential of the cell sap determines its value.
mcqs.specStatementText: Solute and pressure potentials add up: ψw = ψs + ψp
mcqs.explain: Solute potential ranges from zero downwards. Pressure potential is generally positive inside cells, where the wall presses on the contents, but in xylem vessels the sap is pulled up under tension, which is a negative pressure.
rationales: A student who has only met pushing pressures picks this. A column of xylem sap being pulled upward is under tension, and tension is a negative pressure potential.

Solute potential ranges from zero downwards. Pressure potential is generally positive inside cells, where the wall presses on the contents, but in xylem vessels the sap is pulled up under tension, which is a negative pressure.
A student who expects solute to raise the value picks this. Solutes lower the free energy of water, so solute potential is negative in cell sap and in every other solution.
A student who keeps the Standard Level solute-only model picks this. For a cell with a wall, ψw = ψs + ψp, and the pressure potential can be several hundred kilopascals.

mcqs.q: Plant tissue is bathed in pure water. Which statement explains, in terms of solute and pressure potentials, why net uptake of water by its cells eventually stops?
options: Water enters until the cell wall has been stretched to its limit, and the fully stretched wall then physically prevents any more water from passing into the cell.
Uptake does not stop: water keeps entering until the pressure potential exceeds what the wall can withstand and the cell bursts.
Water entering raises the pressure potential as the wall resists expansion, until it cancels the solute potential and the cell's water potential is zero.
Water enters until the cell sap has become so dilute that its solute potential has risen to zero, matching the pure water outside.
mcqs.specStatementText: Explaining turgor and plasmolysis with potentials
mcqs.explain: As water enters, the wall presses back with increasing force, so ψp rises. When ψp equals the magnitude of ψs, ψw = ψs + ψp = 0, equal to the pure water outside; there is no longer a gradient and the cell is at full turgor.
rationales: A student who pictures the cell as a full container picks this. Water crosses the membrane according to water potential, not available space; it is the rising pressure potential that removes the gradient.
A student who transfers bursting from animal cells picks this. The wall withstands the pressure; net uptake stops when the cell's water potential has risen to zero, well before any bursting.

As water enters, the wall presses back with increasing force, so ψp rises. When ψp equals the magnitude of ψs, ψw = ψs + ψp = 0, equal to the pure water outside; there is no longer a gradient and the cell is at full turgor.

A student who thinks only solutes matter picks this. The sap is diluted only slightly; its solute potential stays negative, and equilibrium is reached because the pressure potential rises to cancel it.

mcqs.q: Plant tissue is bathed in a sucrose solution with a water potential of −2500 kPa. The cells initially have a solute potential of −900 kPa and a pressure potential of +600 kPa. Which statement explains what happens?
options: Water leaves the cells; pressure potential becomes negative as the shrinking protoplast pulls inward on the cell wall that surrounds it.
Water leaves the cells; the wall contracts with the protoplast, so the pressure potential stays positive as the cell shrinks.
Water leaves the cells; the sap becomes more concentrated, so ψs rises above zero and the water potential of every cell becomes positive.
Water leaves the cells; pressure potential falls to zero as the protoplast pulls away from the wall, so ψw equals ψs for each cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Explaining turgor and plasmolysis with potentials
mcqs.explain: The cells start at ψw = −900 + 600 = −300 kPa, far above the solution's −2500 kPa, so water leaves. As the protoplast shrinks the wall stops pressing on it, ψp falls to zero and the cells plasmolyse; from incipient plasmolysis onward ψw = ψs, which becomes more negative as the sap concentrates.
rationales: A student who applies xylem tension to any cell under strain picks this. Once the protoplast shrinks away from the wall there is no wall pressure on it, so the pressure potential is zero, not negative.
A student who thinks the whole cell shrinks like a crenating animal cell picks this. The rigid wall keeps its shape; the protoplast pulls away from it and the pressure potential falls to zero.

A student who expects concentrated solutions to have positive values picks this. Concentrating the sap makes its solute potential more negative, and the cell's water potential falls towards −2500 kPa.

The cells start at ψw = −900 + 600 = −300 kPa, far above the solution's −2500 kPa, so water leaves. As the protoplast shrinks the wall stops pressing on it, ψp falls to zero and the cells plasmolyse; from incipient plasmolysis onward ψw = ψs, which becomes more negative as the sap concentrates.

mcqs.q: Five potato cylinders were bathed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose for 24 hours. The mean percentage change in mass was −3.0% with a standard deviation of 1.0%; the mean percentage change in length was −2.0% with a standard deviation of 2.5%. What do these data indicate?
options: The mass measurements were more reliable than the length measurements, because the mass repeats were less widely spread around their mean.
The length measurements contained more mistakes, because a larger standard deviation means that more errors were made when the ruler was used.
Every mass repeat lay within 1.0% of the mean and every length repeat within 2.5% of it, because the standard deviations give the range of each set.
The standard deviations show how close each sample mean is to the true mean, so the length mean is less accurate but the spread of the repeats cannot be compared.
mcqs.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
mcqs.explain: Standard deviation describes the spread of the repeats around their mean. The smaller standard deviation for mass shows that those five repeats agreed more closely, so mass is the more reliable measure of the effect of the solution on the tissue; the length repeats were widely scattered.
rationales: Standard deviation describes the spread of the repeats around their mean. The smaller standard deviation for mass shows that those five repeats agreed more closely, so mass is the more reliable measure of the effect of the solution on the tissue; the length repeats were widely scattered.

A student who reads statistical 'error' as 'mistake' picks this. Standard deviation describes the natural spread of the repeats, not faults in technique; a small change in length is hard to resolve with a ruler, so the repeats scatter even when it is used correctly.

A student who reads any measure of spread as a range picks this. Standard deviation is not the limits of the data: it describes the typical spread of the repeats, and some repeats usually lie further from the mean than one standard deviation, so a mass repeat may well have changed by more than 1.0% away from −3.0%.

A student who treats standard deviation and standard error as one statistic picks this. It is standard error that indicates how close a sample mean is to the true mean; standard deviation describes the spread of the repeats, which is exactly what allows the reliability of the two measurements to be compared.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Standard deviation and standard error are treated only as tools for interpreting the results of the plant-tissue experiment: what each statistic indicates, how the two differ, and how standard error can be shown as error bars. No concept, misconception or item asks for the formula for either statistic or requires a student to calculate one from raw data; q07 supplies the values already computed and asks what they mean.
